kurz: How to structure decisions so that they hold up even if your assessment is wrong.

bloecke.md:
Three quantities play a role in decisions under uncertainty: the probability of being right, the size of the outcome and the cost of reversing the decision. According to the findings of forecasting research, the first quantity can hardly be improved. The second and third, on the other hand, can be shaped almost at will, and in advance.

A useful decision rule therefore starts with the structure of the decision and not with a better forecast. It clarifies which decision still holds up even if your own assessment is wrong, and what it costs to reverse that decision.

## One-way door and two-way door

The distinction became widely known through Jeff Bezos's 2015 letter to shareholders. In it, Type 1 decisions are one-way doors through which there is no way back, or only at high cost. Type 2 decisions are two-way doors. If you notice a mistake, you go back and carry on.

Gut feeling is of little help in the classification, because people easily confuse importance with finality. The distinction only becomes useful with a number, the [[Reversal costs|reversal costs]]. These include everything that returning to the starting position costs: taxes, fees, cancellation charges, lapsed deadlines and lost time. They are measured as a percentage of the amount invested. If they are below about 1% and the decision can be unwound within a few days, it is a two-way door. Then lengthy deliberation is already a mistake. If they are higher, it is a [[One-way door decision|one-way door decision]], and every hour of thought is justified.

bloecke.md:
The portfolio holds €40,000 in an accumulating world ETF, of which €12,000 is book gain. An almost identical ETF costs 0.10 percentage points less a year. The switch appears reversible because you could buy back at any time.

The sale, however, realises the gain. After the 30% partial exemption (Teilfreistellung) for equity funds (Section 20 InvStG, Investment Tax Act), €8,400 is taxable. After deducting the full saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000 (Section 20(9) EStG), €7,400 remains. On this, 26.375% flat-rate withholding tax and solidarity surcharge is due. That is around €1,952, not including church tax. So €38,048 instead of €40,000 is reinvested, a shortfall of 4.9%.

A cost advantage of 0.10 percentage points a year takes around 50 years to close this gap. At 0.30 percentage points, it still takes around 17 years. The switch therefore looks like a two-way door but is a one-way door. Buying back is possible at any time, but that does not bring back the tax already paid.

The familiar mistake is to walk through a one-way door too quickly. More common is the opposite mistake of examining a two-way door for so long that the time spent was more expensive than any possible error. Both mistakes have the same cause. In both cases, the type of door was never determined.

## Statutory periods for reflection

German law recognises the distinction and provides periods for reflection above all where reversal becomes expensive. A contract for financial services concluded at a distance can be revoked within 14 days under Sections 312c and 355 BGB (Civil Code). For life and pension insurance, Section 152(1) VVG extends the period to 30 days, because the cancellation costs are considerable there. For property purchases, Section 17(2a) sentence 2 no. 2 BeurkG (Notarisation Act) stipulates that, as a rule, consumers must have the draft contract two weeks before the notarisation appointment.

Securities transactions are excluded from the right of withdrawal because their price depends on market fluctuations (Section 312g(2) no. 8 BGB). There is therefore no statutory period for reflection when buying shares or ETFs, only a self-imposed one. This gap is closed by cooling-off periods that you set in writing before the first urge to buy arises, for example one night for four-digit amounts and one week for five-digit amounts.

## Decision quality and outcome

A decision is made before the outcome. It can therefore only be judged by what was known at the time of the decision. If it is instead assessed backwards from the outcome, this is known as [[Resulting|resulting]]. Such a judgement draws conclusions from a sample of one. For money decisions, this is particularly useless, because chance accounts for a very large share of any single outcome.

bloecke.titel: Process and outcome as separate judgements

bloecke.md: In 1975, Fischhoff demonstrated that people shift their own prior assessment, in hindsight, towards the outcome that actually occurred. After the event, therefore, nobody knows their original expectation any more. Without a dated note, it is impossible to determine in which field of the matrix a decision lay. Corrections to the approach are then based mainly on random fluctuations.

## Ranges instead of point estimates

The second systematic form of overconfidence is [[Overprecision|overprecision]]. Here people set their forecast intervals too narrowly. Alpert and Raiffa (1982) and Lichtenstein and colleagues showed that intervals which were supposed to contain the true value with 98% probability contained it considerably less often.

Experts do no better. Between 2018 and 2025, the consensus forecast of Wall Street strategists for the S&P 500 was within plus or minus ten percentage points of the result in only one of eight years. It was furthest off in 2022, with an expected plus 3.9% against a result of minus 19.4%, a deviation of 23.3 percentage points. A single forecast figure is therefore not usable information, even if it looks precise.

bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation using the extreme values of all 20-year windows in the DAX return triangle over 50 years (as of 31 December 2025), before costs and taxes. There is almost a factor of nine between the worst and the best window.

bloecke.md:
In practice, this means that a plan is tested at the lower end of the range and not at the mean. A withdrawal plan, a mortgage loan or a retirement goal that only works out at 8.4% a year fails in roughly half of all conceivable paths. Such a plan is only sustainable if it also works out at 3.3%, if necessary with a longer term, a lower withdrawal or a buffer that does not depend on the market.

Kostolany expressed the same insight more concisely. His sentence describes the path to the result more than the result itself. What is expected does happen, but only after an interim loss that you must be able to withstand.

bloecke.text: At the stock exchange, two times two is never four, but five minus one.

bloecke.md: Instead of “the fund will make 7%”, it is better to note a 90% interval such as “between minus 4% and plus 17%”. The range is then doubled, because empirically intervals are always set too narrowly. Only with this range do you check whether the decision holds up. A forecast without a lower limit is not fit to serve as the basis for a decision.

## Precommitment and triggers

With a [[Precommitment|precommitment]], the action is determined while the situation is calm. A genuine commitment differs from a resolution in three specifics: an observable trigger, a concrete action and an execution date. “I will stay invested even in a crash” is a resolution. “If the portfolio value falls by more than 25%, nothing is sold, and the savings plan contribution continues automatically on the 1st of the month” is a commitment. Its execution is already set up before the situation arises.

schritte.text: Estimate the reversal costs in euros and express them as a percentage of the amount invested. If they are below around 1%, decide immediately and move on.
Assume a bad, a medium and a good path. The only test is whether the plan can also bear the bad figure.
Write down which observation would prove the decision wrong, and set a date on which to check. Without this criterion, any later evaluation is arbitrary.
For Type 1 decisions, the statutory withdrawal period is a free option. It is planned in for the review from the outset and not merely waited out.
Note the date, assumption, range and trigger. Without this record, only memory remains for the later assessment, and memory is demonstrably distorted.

bloecke.md:
## Value of additional research

Research always feels like diligence. Three tests, answered before the research, show whether it actually is.

The **change test** asks which result of the research would change the action. If this cannot be formulated in advance, the research only serves as confirmation and yields no gain in knowledge.

The **price test** checks whether the information is public and the market liquid. In that case, it is already reflected in the price. In 1999, Odean analysed around 163,000 transactions from 10,000 securities accounts. Twelve months later, the shares bought lagged behind the shares sold by 3.3 percentage points on average. The additional work therefore had a negative return.

The **proportionality test** compares the research time with the reversal costs. With a two-way door, a mistake is cheaper than the review.

bloecke.titel: Success rate of active funds by fund category
bloecke.unter: Share of active US funds that survived over ten years and beat their passive counterpart (Morningstar Active/Passive Barometer, as of 30 June 2025). The more liquid and public the market, the less research pays off.

bloecke.md:
A checklist protects against omissions but not against errors of judgement. It does not replace analysis, but it prevents a known point from being forgotten under time pressure.

Two designs need to be distinguished. With a read-do list, each point is carried out in turn before moving on. This makes sense for processes with a fixed sequence, such as setting up a savings plan. With a do-confirm list, you work freely and check against the list at the end. This makes sense for decisions that involve discretion.

A checklist becomes effective through three rules: at most around seven to nine points, each point formulated in observable terms (“expense ratio and fund size noted” instead of “costs checked”) and at least one point at which you occasionally fail. A list that never holds anyone up has no checking effect.

In 2007, Bar-Eli and colleagues analysed a total of 286 penalty kicks. Goalkeepers almost always dive to the left or right, even though staying in the centre would give a higher save rate. The reason for this is not ignorance. For goalkeepers, a goal conceded after diving is easier to bear than one conceded while standing still. The same mechanism operates on the stock exchange, but there fees and taxes come on top. That is why “do nothing” belongs on every decision list as an explicitly examined and recorded option. Otherwise, this option is never weighed on an equal footing with acting.

mitnehmen: Forecasting accuracy can hardly be improved, whereas reversal costs and position size can be shaped almost at will; that is why work pays off above all on these two quantities.
First determine the type of door, because with reversal costs below about 1%, lengthy deliberation is already a mistake, while with higher costs every hour of thought is justified.
The ETF switch with a book gain of €12,000 costs around €1,952 in tax, and a cost advantage of 0.10 percentage points takes around 50 years to make up this amount.
A plan is tested at the lower end of the range and not at the mean; for the DAX, the 20-year windows range from 3.3% to 15.2% a year.
A decision is judged by what was known beforehand, and after the event this is only possible with a dated note.

begriffe.text: Decision that is impossible or expensive to reverse (Type 1). Its counterpart is the two-way door (Type 2), where returning to the starting position costs almost nothing.
All costs incurred when a decision is reversed, that is, taxes, fees, cancellation charges, lapsed deadlines and time spent. They are measured as a percentage of the amount invested.
Evaluating a decision by its outcome instead of by the information that was available when the decision was made. Resulting means that bad decisions which happened to turn out well are repeated.
Form of overconfidence in which forecast intervals are systematically set too narrowly. An interval described as 90% certain contains the true value considerably less often.

Rule with an observable trigger, a specific action and an execution date, which is decided in calm conditions and automated where possible so that it is no longer up for debate in a stressful situation.
